l: Athens, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Athens is a city full of idols, including an altar inscribed 'TO AN UNKNOWN GOD'. Paul, waiting there for Silas and Timothy, is provoked by the idols and reasons daily in synagogue and marketplace among Athenians fond of novelty.

l: Areopagus, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Philosophers took Paul to the Areopagus, asking to know what his new teaching was. Paul stood in its middle and gave his speech there. Dionysius the Areopagite was among those who joined Paul and believed.

l: Caesar, The Acts of the Apostles
s: is_called emperor [Festus's lord] Caesar is the authority to whom Paul appeals, saying he is standing before Caesar's judgment seat, and Festus answers that to Caesar he shall go. Paul denies having sinned against Caesar. Festus says he has nothing certain to write to his lord, referring to the emperor.

l: Jews of Thessalonica, The Acts of the Apostles
s: opposes Paul [stirred crowds against him in Thessalonica and Beroea] The unpersuaded Jews took wicked men from the marketplace, gathered a crowd and set the city in an uproar, assaulting Jason's house and dragging Jason and others before the rulers. They accused Paul's group of turning the world upside down and acting against Caesar's decrees. When they learned Paul was preaching in Beroea, they went there and agitated the multitudes.

l: Beroean Jews, The Acts of the Apostles
s: The Jews of Beroea, deemed more noble than Thessalonica's, eagerly received Paul's word and daily examined the Scriptures to verify it, so many believed.

l: Epicurean and Stoic philosophers, The Acts of the Apostles
s: is_a philosophers [Athenian schools] Some Epicurean and Stoic philosophers conversed with Paul in Athens. Some called him a babbler, others said he seemed to advocate foreign deities because he preached Jesus and the resurrection. They took him to the Areopagus to explain his new teaching.

l: Athenians, The Acts of the Apostles
s: The Athenians are a group Paul judges very religious, citing an altar to an unknown god, and who spend their time telling or hearing new things. After his speech, some mocked the resurrection, others wanted more, and some believed.

l: Paul's speech at the Areopagus, The Acts of the Apostles
s: is_delivered_at Areopagus [Paul stood in the middle] Paul began from the altar to an unknown God and declared that the God who made the world does not dwell in temples or need human service. He said God made every nation from one blood to seek him, quoted poets that 'we are also his offspring', argued that the Divine Nature is not like gold, silver or stone, and called all people to repent because of a coming judgment by a man God raised from the dead. Reaction was divided between mockery and a wish to hear more, and some believed.

l: Aquila, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Aquila is a Jewish tentmaker from Pontus, husband of Priscilla, expelled from Rome under Claudius. He hosts and works with Paul, sails with him to Ephesus, and there instructs Apollos with Priscilla.

l: Priscilla, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Priscilla, a tent maker's wife recently from Italy, accompanies Paul and Aquila to Ephesus, stays there, and with Aquila explains God's way more accurately to Apollos.

l: Apollos, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Apollos is an eloquent Alexandrian Jew, mighty in the Scriptures, who comes to Ephesus teaching accurately about Jesus though knowing only John's baptism. Priscilla and Aquila instruct him more fully; encouraged by the brothers, he goes to Achaia, helps believers, and publicly refutes Jews, showing Jesus is the Christ.

l: Gallio, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Gallio, proconsul of Achaia, is indifferent to disputes brought before him. When Jews bring Paul to his judgment seat, he dismisses their case as a matter of their own law, drives them off, and ignores Sosthenes being beaten.

l: Corinth, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Corinth is where Paul meets Aquila and Priscilla, works, and reasons in the synagogue. Crispus, the synagogue ruler, believes with his household, and many Corinthians believe and are baptized. The Lord tells Paul he has many people in this city, and Paul stays there a year and six months.

l: Ephesus, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Ephesus is a city described as temple keeper of the great goddess Artemis and of an image said to have fallen from Zeus. Paul arrives, leaves Priscilla and Aquila, reasons in the synagogue, and promises to return. Apollos is instructed there. Paul later teaches about two years, all Asia hears the word, and Jews and Greeks magnify Jesus' name.

l: charge before Gallio, The Acts of the Apostles
s: alleges worship contrary to the law [brought by the Jews] The Jews claim that Paul persuades men to worship God contrary to the law. Gallio says he would bear with them if it were wrong or wicked crime, but since it concerns words, names, and their own law, he refuses to judge it and drives them from the judgment seat.

l: disciples (certain disciples at Ephesus), The Acts of the Apostles
s: About twelve disciples at Ephesus had received only John's baptism of repentance and knew nothing of the Holy Spirit. After Paul explained, they were baptized in Jesus's name; when he laid hands on them, the Spirit came, and they spoke in languages and prophesied.

l: the Way, The Acts of the Apostles
s: The Way is a religious movement Paul once persecuted to the death, imprisoning men and women. In Chapter 19 some in the synagogue speak evil of it, sparking a disturbance and riot. Later, Paul's accusers call it a sect, while he confesses serving his fathers' God according to it, believing the law and prophets.

l: itinerant Jewish exorcists, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Itinerant Jewish exorcists, including Sceva's seven sons, try casting out an evil spirit by invoking Jesus whom Paul preaches; the spirit disowns them, and the possessed man overpowers them, leaving them fleeing naked and wounded.

l: evil spirit, The Acts of the Apostles
s: knows Jesus [also knows Paul] An evil spirit answers the exorcists that it knows Jesus and Paul but asks who they are. The man it possessed leaps on the seven, overpowers them, and prevails so that they flee the house naked and wounded. Elsewhere evil spirits go out of the sick when handkerchiefs or aprons from Paul's body are carried to them.

l: burning of magical books, The Acts of the Apostles
s: has_value fifty thousand pieces of silver [price counted] After the exorcists' failure, many believers confess their deeds, and many who practiced magical arts bring their books together and burn them in the sight of all. The books are counted as worth fifty thousand pieces of silver, and the word of the Lord grows and becomes mighty.

l: Demetrius, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Demetrius is a silversmith making silver shrines of Artemis, whose work brings craftsmen business; he rallies them against Paul, whose teaching threatens their trade and Artemis's temple and majesty.

l: craftsmen, The Acts of the Apostles
s: derives_wealth_from silver shrines of Artemis [their business] The craftsmen and workmen of like occupation are gathered by Demetrius, who reminds them their wealth comes from the shrine business. They fill with anger and cry out, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!"

l: Artemis, The Acts of the Apostles
s: is_worshipped_by Asia [also the world; called great goddess] Artemis is the great goddess of the Ephesians, whom all Asia and the world are said to worship, and whose temple and silver shrines support the trade of Demetrius and the craftsmen. Her majesty is said to be threatened by Paul's teaching, and the crowd cries "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!" for about two hours.

l: Ephesian riot, The Acts of the Apostles
s: occurs_in theater (at Ephesus) [crowd rushed there] The city fills with confusion and the people rush into the theater, seizing Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians and Paul's travel companions. Paul is kept from entering by the disciples and Asiarchs, and most in the assembly do not know why they came. The crowd shouts down Alexander, a Jew, and the town clerk finally quiets it and dismisses the assembly.

l: town clerk, The Acts of the Apostles
s: has_role quieting the multitude and dismissing the assembly [official of Ephesus] The town clerk quiets the multitude and says Ephesus is temple keeper of Artemis, so they should be calm and do nothing rash. He says the men seized are neither temple robbers nor blasphemers, directs Demetrius and the craftsmen to the courts and proconsuls, warns they risk accusation over the riot, and dismisses the assembly.

l: crowd of Ephesians, The Acts of the Apostles
s: A crowd of Ephesians rushes confusedly into the theater, most not knowing why. On learning Alexander is a Jew, they shout 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!' for two hours until the town clerk quiets and dismisses them.

l: Eutychus, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Eutychus is a young man at Troas who, weighed down by sleep while Paul spoke at length, fell from a third-floor window and was taken up dead; Paul embraced him, and he was brought in alive, comforting everyone.

l: Miletus, The Acts of the Apostles
s: is_location_of Paul's farewell speech [Paul summoned the Ephesian elders there] Miletus was where the travelers arrived after sailing past Chios, Samos, and Trogyllium. From there Paul sent to Ephesus for the elders of the assembly and delivered his farewell speech to them. The ship waiting there was where the elders accompanied him at the end.

l: elders of the assembly (Ephesus), The Acts of the Apostles
s: Elders of Ephesus, made overseers by the Holy Spirit to shepherd the flock. Paul summoned them to Miletus, warned of wolves and perverse men arising among them, said they'd not see him again; they wept, embraced him, and escorted him to the ship.

l: Paul's farewell speech, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Paul's farewell speech at Miletus, addressed to the elders of the assembly at Ephesus. He recounts his humble, tearful service in Asia and his teaching publicly and house to house, declares himself clean of all blood, warns that wolves will come, entrusts the elders to God, and quotes Jesus on giving.

l: Paul's companions (we), The Acts of the Apostles
s: The narrator's group travels with Paul from Cos through Rhodes, Patara, Tyre, Ptolemais, and Caesarea, staying with disciples and with Philip the evangelist. They beg Paul with the local people not to go up to Jerusalem, then cease, saying 'The Lord's will be done,' and go with him to Jerusalem, where the brothers receive them gladly and they meet James.

l: vow and purification, The Acts of the Apostles
s: The elders propose that Paul join four men who have taken a vow, purify himself with them, and pay their expenses so they may shave their heads, showing that he keeps the law. Paul does so, entering the temple the next day to declare the days of purification until offerings are made for each man. The seven days are almost complete when he is seized.

l: the Jews, The Acts of the Apostles
s: The Jews are a group made up of twelve tribes who hold a hope in the promise God made to their fathers. The records chiefly show their hostility toward Paul. It begins in the temple, where Jews from Asia seize him, stir up the crowd, and accuse him of teaching against the people, the law, and the place, and of bringing Greeks inside, wrongly assuming Trophimus was with him. Then more than forty bind themselves under a curse to neither eat nor drink until Paul is killed, but their plan is discovered. Next the high priest and principal men press Festus to send Paul to Jerusalem, plotting to kill him on the way, and bring grievous charges they cannot prove. The whole multitude cries that he should not live. Finally Paul says they accuse him over the hope of the promise and tried to kill him in the temple.

l: crowd, The Acts of the Apostles
s: The crowd runs together, seizes Paul, drags him out of the temple, and tries to kill him, stopping the beating only when the soldiers appear. Its members shout conflicting things, so the officer cannot learn the truth, and they follow crying 'Away with him!' until Paul gains a great silence by beckoning from the stairs.

l: commanding officer (Claudius Lysias), The Acts of the Apostles
s: Claudius Lysias is the commanding officer of the regiment, who commands soldiers and centurions. When Jerusalem erupts in an uproar, he rushes down, stops the beating, arrests Paul, has him chained, and lets him address the crowd. He orders Paul scourged, then becomes afraid on learning Paul is a Roman he had bound; he frees him and convenes the chief priests and council. Fearing Paul would be torn apart, he takes him into the barracks. After hearing of a plot from Paul's nephew, he sends Paul to Felix under heavy armed escort by night, with a letter stating Paul faced no charge worthy of death or imprisonment.

l: uproar in Jerusalem and Paul's arrest, The Acts of the Apostles
s: After Asian Jews accuse Paul in the temple, all the city is moved and the people seize him and try to kill him. The commanding officer intervenes, has Paul chained, and cannot learn the cause from the shouting, so he orders Paul carried up the stairs by soldiers because of the crowd's violence. Paul is then allowed to address the people.

l: the crowd (Jerusalem), The Acts of the Apostles
s: is_hostile_to Paul [demanded his death] The crowd grows quieter when Paul speaks in Hebrew and listens until he mentions being sent to the Gentiles. They then cry out for him to be removed from the earth as unfit to live, throwing off cloaks and tossing dust into the air.

l: scourging of Paul, The Acts of the Apostles
s: ordered_by commanding officer (Jerusalem barracks) [to learn the crime for which they shouted against him] The commanding officer orders Paul examined by scourging, and Paul is tied with straps. It is halted before it begins when Paul asks whether it is lawful to scourge an uncondemned Roman, and those about to examine him depart.

l: Roman citizenship, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Roman citizenship is a legal status protecting against uncondemned scourging. Paul invokes it, the commanding officer admits buying his for a great price while Paul was born Roman, and the officer fears having bound him.

l: council, The Acts of the Apostles
s: A council made of Sadducees and Pharisees; after hearing Paul it divides into a great argument over the resurrection, and conspirators then plan to have it request Paul's return pretending to examine his case.

l: Felix, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Felix is a governor at Caesarea, married to Drusilla, long a judge of the Jews and knowing the Way more exactly. He receives Paul and Lysias's letter, keeps Paul in Herod's palace, and defers the case. Terrified by Paul's talk of judgment, he still hopes for a bribe. After two years Porcius Festus succeeds him, and Felix leaves Paul in bonds to win favor with the Jews.

l: young man (Paul's sister's son), The Acts of the Apostles
s: is_relative_of Paul [sister's son] Paul's sister's son hears that the conspirators are lying in wait, goes into the barracks, and tells Paul. A centurion brings him to the commanding officer, to whom he reveals the plot and the request the Jews will make. The commanding officer lets him go with a charge to tell no one.

l: plot to kill Paul, The Acts of the Apostles
s: planned_location on the way to Jerusalem [ambush] More than forty men plan an ambush to kill Paul by having the council ask for him to be brought down on the pretense of a more exact inquiry. The plot is revealed by Paul's sister's son, and the commanding officer defeats it by sending Paul away at night to Caesarea under armed escort.

l: resurrection of the dead, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Resurrection of the dead is presented as a doctrine taught by Moses and the prophets, with Christ to be first to rise. Paul's trial centers on it: in Chapter 23 it divides Pharisees, who affirm resurrection, angel and spirit, from Sadducees, who deny them. In Chapter 24 he hopes in God for the resurrection of the just and unjust. In Chapter 26 he calls it credible and tied to the fathers' promise, Christ proclaiming light.

l: Tertullus, The Acts of the Apostles
s: is_a orator [spoke for the accusers] Tertullus, an orator, speaks for the accusers, flattering Felix for the peace and prosperity under his foresight. He accuses Paul of being a plague, an instigator of insurrections among Jews throughout the world, a ringleader of the Nazarenes, and one who tried to profane the temple.

l: Festus, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Festus is the Roman governor who succeeds Felix. Arriving in the province, he goes to Jerusalem, refuses the Jews' request to move Paul there, and hears the case at Caesarea. Hoping to please the Jews, he asks Paul about trial in Jerusalem, then sends him to Caesar. He presents Paul to King Agrippa, calls Paul crazy during his defense, and hears Agrippa say Paul could have been freed.

l: Paul's trial before Felix, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Paul's trial before Felix opens with accusations from Ananias, the elders, and Tertullus, and Paul's denial of the charges. Felix defers judgment until Lysias comes, never decides, and after two years leaves Paul in bonds as Festus succeeds him.

l: King Agrippa, The Acts of the Apostles
s: King Agrippa is a king, accompanied by Bernice and known as an expert in Jewish customs and questions. He arrives at Caesarea, greets Festus, and asks to hear Paul. He attends the hearing with great pomp, permits Paul to speak, asks if Paul is trying to make him a Christian, and says Paul might have been freed had he not appealed to Caesar.

l: Paul's appeal to Caesar, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Paul's appeal to Caesar: asked whether he'll be judged in Jerusalem, Paul insists he should be tried where he stands and appeals to Caesar; Festus, after conferring with the council, grants it and keeps Paul in custody until sending him.

l: Paul's trial, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Paul's trial at Caesarea, presided over by Festus on the judgment seat: Jews from Jerusalem press charges, Paul defends himself and rejects moving the case to Jerusalem by appealing, and Festus then arranges a further hearing before Agrippa.

l: charges against Paul, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Charges against Paul are many and grievous but unproven; Paul denies offending Jewish law, the temple, or Caesar. Festus finds them to be disputes about religion and a dead Jesus Paul claims is alive, finds nothing deserving death, and plans to specify charges.

l: Paul's defense, The Acts of the Apostles
s: is_made_before King Agrippa [concerning accusations by the Jews] Paul's defense before Agrippa covers his Pharisee life, his persecution of the saints, his vision at Damascus, and his preaching of repentance, which he says is nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would happen. It is interrupted by Festus, and afterward Agrippa, Festus, Bernice and the others agree Paul does nothing worthy of death or bonds.

l: Julius, The Acts of the Apostles
s: Julius, a centurion of the Augustan band, takes custody of Paul and other prisoners, treats Paul kindly at Sidon, and boards them at Myra. He first follows the ship's master over Paul's warning, later heeds Paul, and spares the prisoners to save Paul.

l: Alexandrian ship, The Acts of the Apostles
s: An Alexandrian ship bound for Italy, found at Myra by the centurion, who boards Paul and others. It sails slowly, leaves Fair Havens, is driven by the Euroclydon wind, is lightened of cargo, and finally runs aground, its stern breaking up.

l: Euroclydon, The Acts of the Apostles
s: is_a stormy wind Euroclydon is the stormy wind that beats down from shore shortly after a gentle south wind lures the ship along Crete. It catches the ship, which cannot face it, and drives it along for many days without sun or stars, until all hope of being saved is lost.

l: sailors, The Acts of the Apostles
s: The sailors, along with the master and owner, are the ones the majority follow in deciding to leave Fair Havens. At midnight on the fourteenth night they sense land, take soundings of twenty and then fifteen fathoms, and drop four anchors from the stern. They try to flee in the boat under the pretense of laying out bow anchors, but Paul exposes this and the soldiers cut the boat away.

l: soldiers, The Acts of the Apostles
s: The soldiers cut away the ropes of the boat and let it fall off after Paul warns that the sailors must stay aboard. When the ship runs aground, they counsel killing the prisoners so none can swim away and escape, but the centurion stops them.

l: people aboard the ship, The Acts of the Apostles
s: has_count 276 The 276 people aboard endure the storm, throw cargo and tackle overboard, and go long without food. Encouraged by Paul, they eat, then lighten the ship further by throwing out the wheat. When the ship breaks up, they all reach land safely, some swimming and the rest on planks and other things from the ship.

l: shipwreck on the island, The Acts of the Apostles
s: A ship runs aground where two seas meet after the crew, not recognizing the land, tries to drive it onto a beach in a bay. The bow sticks fast while the stern breaks up in the waves. Paul's prediction is fulfilled and everyone escapes safely ashore.

l: Malta, The Acts of the Apostles
s: is_a island Malta is the island the escaped party learns they have reached. Its natives show kindness, Publius holds lands there, and the sick of the island are cured; the party stays three months and a ship of Alexandria that had wintered there carries them on.

l: natives of Malta, The Acts of the Apostles
s: shows uncommon kindness [toward the shipwrecked party] The natives show uncommon kindness by kindling a fire for the survivors because of the rain and cold. They first take Paul's viper bite as a sign he is a murderer, then call him a god when he is unharmed, and they honor the party and supply their needs when they sail.

l: Jewish leaders in Rome, The Acts of the Apostles
s: views this sect [known to be spoken against everywhere] Paul calls together the Jewish leaders, and they say they have received no letters or evil reports about him but know the sect is spoken against everywhere. They set a day, hear him from morning till evening, and are divided, some believing and some not. They depart in great dispute after Paul quotes Isaiah about their callous hearts.

l: salvation of God, The Acts of the Apostles
s: is_sent_to nations [and they will listen] Paul declares to the Jewish leaders that the salvation of God is sent to the nations, and that they will listen. He says this after quoting Isaiah on a people whose hearts have grown callous.

l: The Letter to the Hebrews
s: The document is the Letter to the Hebrews, thirteen chapters of exhortation and argument addressed to 'brothers' who are tempted to drift or shrink back. Its central figure is Jesus, the Son of God, whom the author presents as superior to every earlier mediator. Chapter 1 opens by saying God, who spoke through the prophets, has now spoken through his Son, who is heir of all things, radiance of God's glory, and better than the angels, as a chain of quoted statements shows. Chapter 2 warns against neglecting so great a salvation. Jesus was made lower than the angels, tasted death for everyone, freed those enslaved by fear of death, and became a merciful and faithful high priest. Chapters 3 and 4 set Jesus above Moses, who was a servant in the house while Christ is Son over it. They recall the wilderness generation that failed to enter God's rest through unbelief, and say a Sabbath rest remains for God's people. Jesus is a great high priest who sympathizes with weakness, so believers may approach the throne of grace. Chapters 5 to 7 develop his priesthood. He was called by God as Aaron was, a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek, who blessed Abraham and received tithes from him. The author rebukes readers for needing milk instead of solid food, urges them on to maturity, warns about falling away, and offers hope as an anchor of the soul. Jesus holds an unchangeable priesthood and offered himself once for all. Chapters 8 to 10 contrast the old and new covenants. The earthly tabernacle and repeated sacrifices were copies and shadows. Christ entered the heavenly tabernacle through his own blood, mediates a better covenant with laws written on hearts and sins remembered no more, and will appear a second time to save those awaiting him. Readers are urged to draw near, hold fast, encourage one another, and not shrink back. Chapter 11 defines faith and surveys examples, from Abel, Noah, and Abraham to Moses and unnamed sufferers, none of whom received the promise, since God provided something better for 'us.' Chapter 12 calls readers to run with perseverance looking to Jesus, to accept hardship as a Father's discipline, and to avoid Esau's example. They have come to Mount Zion rather than the terrifying mountain, and are to serve God with reverence because he is a consuming fire. Chapter 13 closes with practical commands: brotherly love, hospitality, honoring marriage, freedom from the love of money, and obedience to leaders. Since Jesus is the same yesterday, today, and forever, readers should go out to him outside the camp. The letter ends with a request for prayer, news of Timothy, greetings, and a blessing.

l: God, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: God, as presented in the Letter to the Hebrews, is the living, faithful, and truthful creator and judge who speaks, promises, and disciplines. The records open by saying he spoke to the fathers through the prophets and, at the end of these days, through his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things and through whom he made the worlds. He is the source and means of all things, the builder of all things, and the one who frames the universe by his word. Early chapters show him testifying to salvation with signs and wonders, bringing many children to glory, and appointing Jesus. He is displeased with the wilderness generation that tested him and swears in wrath that they will not enter his rest, which he himself entered on the seventh day. All creatures are open to his sight and must give account. He calls and appoints the high priest, declares Christ a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek, and saved Christ from death. He is not unrighteous, blesses fruitful land, and cannot lie: he confirmed his promise to Abraham by an oath, swearing by himself. Under the new covenant he takes no pleasure in the old sacrifices, prepares a body for the one who comes to do his will, puts his laws on hearts and minds, and remembers sins no more. He is faithful, claims vengeance and judgment, and is the living God into whose hands it is fearful to fall. Faith pleases him; he rewards those who seek him. He is not ashamed to be called the God of those who desire a heavenly country, and he has prepared a city for them. Near the end he is the Father of spirits who disciplines those he loves for their profit, the Judge of all, and a consuming fire who warns from heaven and will shake earth and heavens. The close presents him as the God of peace who brought Jesus back from the dead, who promises never to leave or forsake the readers, who is pleased by sacrifices of doing good and sharing, and who is asked to make them complete in every good work, with glory forever.

l: Jesus, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: Jesus, called the Son, is presented across chapters 1-4, 6 and 7 of the Letter to the Hebrews as superior to angels and Moses and as the perfected, eternal high priest. He is appointed heir of all things, the radiance of God's glory and image of his substance, who upholds all things by the word of his power. He laid the earth's foundation, made the heavens, and remains the same forever while they perish. He is addressed as God with an everlasting throne and scepter of uprightness, loves righteousness and hates iniquity, and is anointed above his fellows. After purifying sins he sits at the right hand of the Majesty on high, awaiting the time his enemies become his footstool. The account then turns to his humanity. He was made a little lower than the angels, shared flesh and blood, and tasted death for everyone. Through death he brings the devil to nothing, and he is crowned with glory and honor. Made perfect through sufferings, he is the author of salvation, calls the offspring of Abraham brothers without shame, and can help the tempted because he was tempted himself. He is a merciful, faithful, sympathetic and sinless high priest who has passed through the heavens. He is called Apostle and High Priest of the readers' confession, faithful as a Son over God's house, and worthy of more glory than Moses. The final movement concerns his priesthood. He entered within the veil as a forerunner and is a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek, though he descends from Judah, a tribe about which Moses said nothing concerning priesthood. He was made priest with an oath sworn by God and is guarantee of a better covenant. Because he lives forever, his priesthood is unchangeable, and he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him. He is holy, guiltless, undefiled, separated from sinners and higher than the heavens, the Son perfected forever.

l: angels, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: Angels are spiritual beings presented in Hebrews as lesser than the Son. God makes them winds and flames of fire, and they serve as spirits sent to those who will inherit salvation. They are commanded to worship the firstborn, were never called Son, and spoke a word whose transgressions were justly penalized. The world to come was not subjected to them, humans and Jesus were made a little lower than them, and Jesus helps Abraham's offspring, not angels.

l: readers (addressees of the letter), The Letter to the Hebrews
s: The readers are the addressees of a letter, a community of believers addressed as brothers. They have Jesus as high priest, a confession to hold tightly, hope as refuge, and bold access to the holy place through his blood. The letter unfolds in three movements. In chapter 4 they are urged to enter God's rest, avoid disobedience, and approach the throne of grace for mercy. In chapter 6 the author, though stern, is persuaded of better things for them, notes God will not forget their service to the saints, and urges diligence and imitation of those who inherited the promises. In chapter 10 they are urged to draw near in full faith, encourage love and good works, and keep assembling. They are reminded of past suffering after enlightenment, including compassion for the author in chains and joyful loss of possessions, and are told to keep their boldness, endure, and not shrink back.

l: salvation, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: Salvation is a so-great matter that neglecting it leaves no escape. It was first spoken through the Lord, confirmed by those who heard, and testified by God with signs, wonders, powers, and Holy Spirit gifts; Jesus, perfected through sufferings, is its author.

l: Abraham, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: Abraham is a patriarch who holds God's promises of blessing and multiplication, and he obtained them after patiently enduring. He gave Melchizedek a tenth of the plunder and was blessed by him, showing he is the lesser, and Levi is said to have paid tithes in his body. Called by God, he obeyed and went out not knowing where, living as an alien in tents with fellow heirs Isaac and Jacob while seeking God's city. Tested, he offered up his only born son Isaac, trusting God could raise the dead; though as good as dead, he fathered descendants numerous as the stars.

l: offspring of Abraham, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: is_helped_by Jesus [not angels] The offspring of Abraham are those to whom Jesus gives help, in contrast to angels, who are not helped. This is the reason he was made like his brothers in all things.

l: man (humanity), The Letter to the Hebrews
s: is_made_lower_than angels [a little lower, crowned with glory and honor] Quoting a psalm, the text says man was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor, and had all things put under his feet, though not yet seen so. The children, as humanity, share flesh and blood, were subject to bondage through fear of death, and are brought to glory through Jesus, who tasted death for everyone.

l: devil, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: has_power_of death The devil is identified as the one who had the power of death. Jesus partook of flesh and blood so that through death he might bring the devil to nothing.

l: death, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: Death is something Jesus tasted for everyone by God's grace, and it is the means by which he brings the devil, who had its power, to nothing. Fear of death had kept people in bondage all their lifetime until Jesus delivered them.

l: those who heard and disobeyed (the Israelites), The Letter to the Hebrews
s: The Israelites are the fathers who left Egypt under Moses, heard God's word, yet rebelled and tested him for forty years while seeing his deeds. Because they erred in heart and lacked faith, the good news did not profit them. God, displeased, swore in wrath that they would not enter his rest. Their bodies fell in the wilderness, a result of unbelief and disobedience.

l: Moses, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: Moses is a figure presented as faithful in all God's house as a servant, though shown to have less glory than Jesus. Hidden as a child by his parents, who did not fear the king's command, he grew up and refused to be called Pharaoh's daughter's son. He chose ill treatment with God's people, counted the reproach of Christ greater than Egypt's treasures, left Egypt by faith, kept the Passover, and led the people out, many of whom rebelled.

l: house (God's house), The Letter to the Hebrews
s: The house is the one in which Moses was faithful as a servant and over which Christ is faithful as a Son. Its builder has more honor than the house, and the text says 'we are his house' if we hold fast our confidence and the glorying of our hope firm to the end.

l: readers (the audience addressed), The Letter to the Hebrews
s: The readers are the audience addressed as holy brothers and partakers of a heavenly calling. In Chapter 3 they are told to consider Jesus, avoid an unbelieving heart and falling away, exhort one another daily, and hold confidence firm to the end to remain God's house and partakers of Christ. In Chapter 12 they are surrounded by witnesses, urged to run with perseverance, endure discipline, pursue peace and holiness, and avoid bitterness and profanity like Esau. Having come to Mount Zion and the sprinkled blood, they receive an unshakable Kingdom and must serve God with reverence.

l: rest (God's rest), The Letter to the Hebrews
s: God's rest is a Sabbath rest for God's people. It was sworn in wrath to be denied the disobedient wilderness generation, who could not enter through unbelief. Joshua did not provide it, so it remains available; believers enter through belief, resting from their own works as God rested from his.

l: rebellion and trial in the wilderness, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: occurs_in wilderness This is the time when the fathers tested and tried God for forty years, even while seeing his deeds. It is cited from the Holy Spirit's words as a warning not to harden hearts, and it was carried out by those who came out of Egypt under Moses.

l: unbelief, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: Unbelief is warned against as an evil heart that leads to falling away from the living God. It is identified as the reason the wilderness generation could not enter God's rest.

l: the word of God, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: The word of God is living and active, sharper than a two-edged sword, piercing soul, spirit, joints and marrow, and able to discern the heart's thoughts and intentions.

l: Christ, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: Christ is presented across these records as the Son of God and a high priest named by God, a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek. He did not glorify himself to take this role. In the days of his flesh he prayed with strong crying and tears, was heard for his godly fear, and though a Son learned obedience through suffering. Made perfect, he became the author of eternal salvation for all who obey him. He is also called the author and perfecter of faith, the mediator of a new covenant, the great shepherd of the sheep, and our Lord. The records describe him as the same yesterday, today, and forever. His central work is a single sacrifice. He came as high priest of the coming good things, passed through the greater and more perfect heavenly tabernacle, and entered the Holy Place once for all through his own blood, obtaining eternal redemption. He offered himself without defect to God through the eternal Spirit, in a body prepared to do God's will, to put away sin. Through that one offering he sanctifies and perfects believers forever. He opened a new and living way through the veil of his flesh and is the great priest over God's house. The account unfolds from his appointment and suffering, to his offering and entry into heaven, to his sitting at God's right hand after the one sacrifice and waiting for his enemies to become his footstool. He endured the cross for the joy set before him, despising its shame, and suffered outside the gate to sanctify the people through his blood. God brought him again from the dead. He will appear a second time, not to deal with sin but to save those eagerly waiting for him.

l: high priest, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: The high priest is a man taken from among men and appointed for them in things pertaining to God, offering gifts and sacrifices for sins. Being surrounded by weakness, he deals gently with the ignorant and wayward, and must offer for his own sins too. He does not claim the honor but is called by God, as Aaron was.

l: Melchizedek, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: Melchizedek is king of Salem and priest of God Most High, whose name means king of righteousness and king of peace. He meets Abraham returning from battle, blesses him, and receives a tenth of the plunder, showing he is greater than Abraham. He is described as without father, mother, or genealogy, with no beginning of days or end of life, made like the Son of God, and a priest continually.

l: recipients (the readers addressed), The Letter to the Hebrews
s: The recipients are readers rebuked as dull of hearing: though they should be teachers by now, they still need re-teaching of basic first principles of God's revelations, requiring milk rather than solid food.

l: milk and solid food (spiritual teaching), The Letter to the Hebrews
s: is_for full grown (mature people) [solid food] Milk stands for the elementary teaching suited to babies, and everyone who lives on milk is not experienced in the word of righteousness. Solid food is for the full grown, who by use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil. The readers are said to need milk rather than solid food.

l: those who fell away (once enlightened), The Letter to the Hebrews
s: A group once enlightened, who tasted the heavenly gift, shared in the Holy Spirit and God's word and coming powers; having fallen away, they cannot be renewed to repentance, as they crucify the Son of God again.

l: land (parable of the land), The Letter to the Hebrews
s: A parable land drinks frequent rain; if it yields a suitable crop it receives God's blessing, but if it bears thorns and thistles it is rejected, near cursing, and ends burned.

l: first principles of Christ, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: Foundational teachings of Christ, to be left behind while pressing on to perfection without relaying the foundation: repentance from dead works, faith toward God, baptisms, laying on of hands, resurrection, eternal judgment.

l: God's promise and oath to Abraham, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: God promised Abraham blessing and multiplication, then swore by himself since none greater existed. Promise and oath, two immutable things in which God cannot lie, give heirs who fled for refuge strong encouragement to hold the hope set before them.

l: hope, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: Hope is portrayed as a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, entering within the veil; it is set before those who fled for refuge, and readers are urged to diligently pursue its fullness to the end.

l: Levitical priesthood, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: The Levitical priesthood is made up of the sons of Levi, who receive tithes from their brothers by law. Its priests are mortal, hindered by death, installed without an oath, and weak, offering daily sacrifices first for their own sins. It could not bring perfection, so another priest was needed, and it is shown inferior to Melchizedek's.

l: first covenant, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: The first covenant is the one the Lord made with Israel's fathers when he led them out of Egypt; they did not continue in it. It brought the Levitical priesthood and tithes, yet made nothing perfect, appointing weak men as high priests. Its commandment is annulled as weak and useless, and the priesthood's change requires a change of law. Found faulty, since a second was sought, it is now obsolete, aging, and near vanishing through the new covenant.

l: tithes, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: is_received_by Melchizedek [from Abraham] The Levites take tithes from their brothers according to the law, yet Abraham gave a tenth to Melchizedek. This is used to show Melchizedek's superiority, since those who die receive tithes in one case while in the other one receives them of whom it is testified that he lives. Levi is said to have paid tithes through Abraham.

l: priesthood of Melchizedek order, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: The priesthood of Melchizedek order is the priesthood named in the testimony 'priest forever.' It rests on the power of an endless life, not a fleshly commandment, and was established with an oath, unlike Levitical priests. It replaces the Aaronic order; Jesus holds it unchangeably.

l: new covenant, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: The new covenant is a better covenant, established on better promises and made by the Lord with the house of Israel and the house of Judah. Its provisions: God's laws put in minds and written on hearts, all knowing him from least to greatest, and mercy with sins remembered no more. Chapter 8 introduces it, with the high priest as mediator, and sets out these promises. Chapter 9 identifies Christ as mediator, whose death redeemed transgressions under the first covenant, so the called receive the eternal inheritance; it is compared to a will, in force after death. Chapter 10 repeats the quoted promise through the Holy Spirit's testimony and concludes that, with remission given, no further offering for sin remains.

l: sacrifice (Jesus' offering of himself), The Letter to the Hebrews
s: occurs once for all [unlike daily sacrifices of other high priests] Jesus, the fitting high priest, does not need to offer sacrifices daily as the other high priests do, first for their own sins and then for the people's. He did this once for all when he offered up himself.

l: the Lord, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: The Lord is a divine figure who pitched the true tabernacle, not man. Finding fault with the first covenant, he promises a new covenant with Israel and Judah: laws in their hearts, himself as their God, mercy, and forgotten sins, having disregarded their unfaithful fathers.

l: greater and more perfect tabernacle (heavenly), The Letter to the Hebrews
s: The greater, more perfect heavenly tabernacle is the true sanctuary, pitched by the Lord, not made with hands nor of this creation. Earthly tabernacle service, patterned for Moses, is only its copy and shadow. Christ passed through it into heaven itself to appear in God's presence for us.

l: earthly tabernacle (the tabernacle Moses made), The Letter to the Hebrews
s: The earthly tabernacle Moses made was a copy of heavenly things. It had two parts: the Holy Place, with lamp stand, table and show bread, and, behind the second veil, the Holy of Holies, with the golden altar of incense and ark. Priests entered the first continually; the high priest alone entered the second yearly. Blood was sprinkled on it and its vessels.

l: house of Israel, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: The house of Israel, with Judah, failed to continue in the first covenant and was disregarded by the Lord, who then promises a new covenant: laws written on hearts, becoming his people, all knowing him.

l: first covenant, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: The first covenant was a system of divine service ordinances and an earthly sanctuary, imposed as fleshly rules until a time of reformation; dedicated with blood by Moses, yet its sacrifices could not perfect worshipers' conscience.

l: high priest (Levitical), The Letter to the Hebrews
s: The Levitical high priest alone enters the Holy of Holies once yearly, bringing blood not his own, offering it for himself and the people's errors; his repeated annual entry contrasts with Christ's single offering of himself.

l: blood, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: Blood is a central element of cleansing and covenant. The first covenant was dedicated with calf and goat blood, and without shedding blood there is no remission. Animal blood sanctifies the flesh, while Christ's blood cleanses the conscience from dead works, and Christ entered the Holy Place through it.

l: sacrifices, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: Sacrifices are treated in Chapter 9: first-covenant gifts and offerings could not perfect the worshiper's conscience and only cleansed copies of heavenly things, which required better sacrifices; Christ's single self-sacrifice puts away sin, unlike repeated yearly offerings.

l: law (Moses' law), The Letter to the Hebrews
s: Moses' law is a shadow of the good to come, not the very image of things, unable to perfect worshipers through yearly sacrifices. Its sacrifices are removed as the first order so the second is established; disregarding it brought death without compassion on two or three witnesses.

l: sacrifices (offered under the law), The Letter to the Hebrews
s: Repeated sacrifices offered under the law by standing priests, year by year and day by day; blood of bulls and goats cannot take away sins, only reminding of them yearly. God did not desire them; Christ's one sacrifice replaces them.

l: sins, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: Sins are not taken away by the blood of bulls and goats, and the law's sacrifices only remind of them each year. Christ's one offering deals with them for good, and God promises to remember them no more, so no further offering for sin is needed. Willfully sinning after receiving knowledge of the truth leaves no sacrifice for sins.

l: author (writer of the letter), The Letter to the Hebrews
s: The letter's author, claiming a good conscience and desire to live honorably, asks readers' prayers, hopes to be restored to them soon, urges them to endure his brief exhortation, and reports Timothy, called brother, is freed and may accompany him.

l: faith, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: leads_to saving of the soul Faith is the basis for drawing near to God in fullness, and the righteous one will live by faith. God has no pleasure in one who shrinks back. The writer says his group is not of those who shrink back to destruction but of those who have faith to the saving of the soul.

l: willful sin and judgment, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: Willful sin after receiving knowledge of the truth leaves no remaining sacrifice for sins, only fearful expectation of judgment and consuming fire against adversaries. Trampling the Son of God, treating the covenant blood as unholy, and insulting the Spirit of grace merits worse punishment than breaking Moses' law; vengeance is the Lord's.

l: faith, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: Faith is defined as assurance of things hoped for and proof of things not seen. It is required to be well pleasing to God. Chapter 11 shows it through a long series of examples, from Abel and Noah to Abraham, Moses, and Rahab, though none received the promise.

l: elders, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: The elders, a group commended for faith, obtained approval; they confessed being strangers and pilgrims, desired a heavenly country, and died in faith without receiving the promises.

l: heavenly country, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: is_a better country The heavenly country is the better country that Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and others desired, as strangers and pilgrims on the earth, rather than the country they had left. Because they seek it, God is not ashamed to be called their God, and he has prepared a city for them.

l: Mount Zion, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: is_associated_with city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem [readers have come to it] Mount Zion is where the readers have come, together with the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. It is associated with innumerable angels, the festal gathering and assembly of the firstborn enrolled in heaven, God the Judge, the spirits of just men made perfect, and Jesus the mediator of a new covenant.

l: mountain (Sinai, that burned with fire), The Letter to the Hebrews
s: Sinai is a touchable mountain that burned with fire, blackness, darkness, storm, a trumpet sound, and a voice of words. Its rule that even an animal touching it be stoned made listeners beg for no more words, and Moses trembled in terror. Readers are told they have not come to it.

l: discipline, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: Discipline is presented as proof of legitimate sonship: God treats readers as true sons, unlike earthly fathers who disciplined briefly as they saw fit. It feels grievous for now, not joyous, but is for their profit, sharing his holiness, and later yields peaceful righteousness.

l: Kingdom that can't be shaken, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: has_attribute unshakable The readers are said to be receiving a Kingdom that can't be shaken. This is set against God's promise to shake earth and heavens once more, which signifies the removal of made things so that what is not shaken may remain. In response, the readers are to have grace and serve God acceptably with reverence and awe.

l: leaders, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: The leaders are those who spoke God's word to the readers and watch over their souls, for which they will give account. The readers are told to remember them, imitate their faith, obey and submit to them, make their work joyful, and greet them.

l: readers (the addressees), The Letter to the Hebrews
s: The readers are addressees of a closing exhortation: seeking the coming city since they have no enduring one, holding an altar, and called to continually offer praise through Jesus and show brotherly love. They receive practical instructions, are urged to go outside the camp, obey leaders, and pray, ending with greetings and blessing.

l: outside the camp, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: Outside the camp is where sin offering animals' bodies are burned; Jesus suffered outside the gate, so readers are urged to go out to him there, bearing reproach, having no enduring city.

l: sacrifice of praise, The Letter to the Hebrews
s: is_a fruit of lips [proclaiming allegiance to his name] The readers are told to offer a sacrifice of praise to God continually through Jesus. It is defined as the fruit of lips that proclaim allegiance to his name, and it is joined with doing good and sharing as sacrifices that please God.

l: Peter’s Second Letter
s: This document is the second letter of Peter, a three-chapter New Testament epistle written by Simon Peter, servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, to fellow believers who share his precious faith. Chapter 1 opens with grace and peace, says God's divine power has granted all that pertains to life and godliness, and urges readers to add virtues to their faith, ending in love, so that their calling and entrance into the eternal Kingdom are secure. Peter says he will keep reminding them because his departure is near. He rests his message on eyewitness testimony of Christ's majesty, including the voice from heaven on the holy mountain, and affirms that prophecy came from men moved by the Holy Spirit. Chapter 2 warns of false teachers who will secretly bring destructive heresies, deny the Master, and exploit people through greed. Past judgments prove punishment is certain: the sinning angels cast into Tartarus, the flood with Noah preserved, and Sodom and Gomorrah destroyed while Lot was delivered. The false teachers are lustful, arrogant, and follow Balaam, promising liberty while enslaved to corruption. Chapter 3 recalls the prophets and apostles, predicts last-days mockers who doubt Christ's coming, explains the Lord's patience and the coming day like a thief, and closes urging holy living and growth in grace and knowledge of Jesus Christ.

l: Simon Peter, Peter’s Second Letter
s: Simon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, writes to fellow believers, urging diligence. He promises to keep reminding them while he lives in his tent, his temporary body, and to ensure remembrance after his departure, citing his eyewitness of Christ's majesty and the heavenly voice.

l: Jesus Christ, Peter’s Second Letter
s: Jesus Christ is presented as Lord and Savior and beloved Son of God, well pleasing to the Father. Knowledge of him multiplies grace and peace and makes believers fruitful. Apostles witnessed his majesty, and he received honor and glory from God. His eternal Kingdom awaits believers. His promised coming is mocked, yet he is patient, not slow, wishing all to repent. Readers are urged to grow in his grace; glory is his now and forever.

l: God, Peter’s Second Letter
s: In these records from Peter's Second Letter, God is the divine power who grants believers all things pertaining to life and godliness, calls them by his own glory and virtue, and gives great promises so they may share the divine nature. As Father, he honored Jesus, whom the Majestic Glory voice declared his beloved Son. Chapter 2 shows God as judge and deliverer: he did not spare sinning angels, cast to Tartarus, or the ancient world, yet preserved Noah with seven others and delivered Lot while turning Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes. He knows how to deliver the godly and keep the unrighteous under punishment. Chapter 3 presents him as creator by his word, forming heavens and earth out of water, destroying the old world by flood, and reserving the present heavens and earth for fire on the day of judgment.

l: recipients of the letter (Peter's readers), Peter’s Second Letter
s: Peter's readers are a group who share a precious faith with the apostles and have received God's exceedingly great promises, having escaped worldly corruption caused by lust. In the first letter they are told to add diligently to their faith, make their calling and election sure, and heed the prophetic word. In the second letter they are stirred to remember the prophets and apostles, live in holiness and godliness, look for new heavens and a new earth, be found in peace, without defect and blameless, avoid the error of the wicked, and grow in grace and knowledge.

l: virtues to add to faith, Peter’s Second Letter
s: A progression of virtues added to faith: moral excellence, knowledge, self-control, perseverance, godliness, brotherly affection, and love. When abounding, they prevent idleness and unfruitfulness in knowing Jesus Christ; lacking them brings blindness, shortsightedness, and forgetting cleansing from old sins.

l: Peter's death (departure), Peter’s Second Letter
s: is_a putting off of his tent [coming swiftly, made clear by Jesus Christ] Peter describes his death as the putting off of his tent, which comes swiftly, as Jesus Christ made clear to him. It motivates him to stir up his readers by reminding them now. He will make every effort so they can remember these things after his departure.

l: transfiguration voice experience, Peter’s Second Letter
s: A voice from the Majestic Glory out of heaven came to Jesus on the holy mountain, heard by Peter and the apostles, declaring him beloved Son, well pleasing; Peter cites it as eyewitness proof against cunningly devised fables.

l: prophecy of Scripture, Peter’s Second Letter
s: Prophecy of Scripture, called the more sure word, is likened to a lamp shining in a dark place that readers do well to heed until the day dawns and the morning star arises in their hearts. Peter says it is not of private interpretation; it came not by man's will but from holy men moved by the Holy Spirit.

l: false teachers, Peter’s Second Letter
s: False teachers are portrayed as covetous deceivers who secretly introduce destructive heresies, deny the Master, and exploit readers with deceptive words. They despise authority, slander dignitaries, follow Balaam's way, and entice people escaping error, promising liberty while enslaved to corruption. Their immoral ways cause the way of truth to be maligned. Their destruction is swift and certain, and the blackness of darkness is reserved for them forever.

l: day of the Lord (judgment), Peter’s Second Letter
s: The day of judgment is the appointed time when the Lord punishes the unrighteous, whom he keeps reserved for it, as he does the sinning angels held in pits of darkness. Past judgments serve as examples that false teachers' destruction will not slumber. It comes as a thief in the night: the heavens pass away with a great noise, the elements dissolve with fervent heat, and the earth is burned up. It is also called the day of God, which believers earnestly desire.

l: mockers (last days), Peter’s Second Letter
s: Mockers who arrive in the last days, following their own lusts. They doubt the promise of his coming, asking where it is and claiming all continues as from creation, while willfully forgetting God's word created heavens and earth and brought the flood.

l: promise of his coming, Peter’s Second Letter
s: is_doubted_by mockers (last days) [claim all things continue as from creation] Mockers question it, pointing to the fact that all things have continued unchanged since the fathers fell asleep. The writer answers that the Lord is not slow but patient, wishing all to come to repentance, and that a day with the Lord is as a thousand years.

l: new heavens and a new earth, Peter’s Second Letter
s: New heavens and a new earth are promised by God, a place where righteousness dwells; believers' hope in it motivates diligence to be found in peace, without defect and blameless.

l: Jude
s: Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, writes to those who are called, urging them to contend earnestly for the faith once delivered to the saints. He warns that certain ungodly men have crept in secretly, turning God's grace into indecency and denying Jesus Christ. Jude cites examples of judgment: the people saved out of Egypt who didn't believe, angels who deserted their dwelling, Sodom and Gomorrah, and Cain, Balaam, and Korah, and he quotes Enoch's prophecy of the Lord's coming to judge the ungodly. He calls the intruders murmurers, mockers, and causers of divisions, as the apostles foretold. He then exhorts the beloved to build themselves up in faith, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep themselves in God's love, show varied compassion to others, and closes with praise to God who is able to keep them from stumbling.

l: Jude, Jude
s: Jude identifies himself as a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, and writes to those who are called. Though eager to write about common salvation, he felt constrained to exhort them to contend for the faith, warn them about intruders, and urge them to build themselves up, closing with a doxology to God.

l: Jesus Christ, Jude
s: Jesus Christ is the one Jude serves, and those called are kept for him. The intruders deny him as the only Master and Lord, the apostles spoke of him beforehand, and believers are to look for his mercy leading to eternal life.

l: God, Jude
s: God the Father sanctifies those who are called, and he is described as our Savior who alone is wise, to whom glory, majesty, dominion and power belong. The text says the Lord saved a people out of Egypt and afterward destroyed unbelievers, keeps deserting angels in everlasting bonds, and will come to execute judgment on all the ungodly; he is able to keep believers from stumbling and present them faultless in great joy.

l: recipients (those called, beloved), Jude
s: The recipients are called, sanctified by God the Father, and kept for Jesus Christ, and Jude wishes them mercy, peace, and love multiplied. They are told to remember the apostles' words, build themselves up on their most holy faith, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep themselves in God's love, and show compassion to some while saving others from the fire with fear.

l: intruders (certain ungodly men), Jude
s: These men crept in secretly, were long ago written about for condemnation, turn God's grace into indecency, and deny Jesus Christ. They defile the flesh, despise authority, slander celestial beings, speak evil of what they don't know, follow the ways of Cain, Balaam, and Korah, and are compared to hidden reefs, waterless clouds, fruitless trees, wild waves, and wandering stars. They are murmurers, mockers, and divisive, sensual people without the Spirit, and blackness of darkness is reserved for them.

l: faith, Jude
s: The faith is described as the one once for all delivered to the saints, and Jude urges the recipients to contend earnestly for it. It is also called their most holy faith, on which they are to keep building themselves up.
